Question: Why do Brits eat turkey on Christmas? (Saw this from Mr. Bean and thought it was a Thanksgiving episode at first.)
Answer: We ate turkey before the Pilgrim Fathers, but it wasn’t the turkey you think. The traditional meal at Christmas was the goose, a bit larger than a chicken. However, for something fancier with a better flavour, an African bird now known as the guineafowl was favoured by those who could afford it. Kora27, CC BY-SA 4.0 <Creative Commons - Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International - CC BY-SA 4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons Because it came to us via the Ottomans, it was called the Turkey bird. Over in the new world, there was a native bird which looked quite similar to this, so the settlers referred to it as a turkey. When these birds were imported, they were American turkeys. As they became available cheaper, they were happily adopted by those who could afford something larger than a chicken.

Question: Why do some sources say that taller victims took longer to die in gas chambers? Or that mothers would hold their babies up high air to breathe air? Yet the same gas was ineffective in WW1 due to it being lighter than air and floating away?
Answer: Hydrogen cyanide was not effective in the field because it was too light. However the original gas chambers were fumigation chambers for killing pests on clothes and beddings. They used a solid slow release agent called Zyklon-B. This was safer for the trained fumigation technicians, since it took some time to build up. The cans were opened and the chamber closed. It was later ventilated before entry to collect the sterilised material. The victims were put in the chamber and the door sealed. The technicians (wearing masks) emptied it in through the ceiling vents, so it fell ultimately on the floor, to slowly release the gas which rose up. The victims would realise this as children or small people succumbed first. Actually, hydrogen cyanide has quite a low odour. In order to protect the technicians, Zyklon B was an improvement with an acrid agent which would be detected if a can was leaking or if a chamber was incompletely ventilated. This made the experience much more physically distressing for Holocaust victims than pure hydrogen cyanide would have been.

Question: Why didn't Europeans sail westward across the Atlantic before Columbus supposedly first did in 1492? Were ships not capable before then? Why?
Answer: The thing that people overlook was the fact that Columbus had a plan for getting back. There were winds to the west, which was OK for going, but to come back against the wind was very hard for a sailing ship. That’s why people did not go farther west. Observing the currents and variations in the winds over the year, he worked out a time and route. This involved going south and taking the winds to the west. He would then need to re-provision with whatever he found, then do the hard work of getting north by what is known as beating against the wind in order to catch winds going east to Europe. Question: Is it true that Britain in WW2 didn’t know how to mass-produce penicillin, and had to count on American production?
Answer: They knew how to manufacture penicillin, but their pharmaceutical industry was fully stretched because of the war and because Germany kept bombing it. So they thought perhaps the USA companies could do the manufacture (and sell it, of course, as they did with other supplies, being neutral). Howard Florey and Norman Heatley went across and showed them the method, but the companies thought it was too risky for investment. However they promised to provide enough for Britain to carry out a proper mass clinical trial, so Florey went home. Heatley stayed and worked at a US research centre, greatly improving the efficiency of production and scaleup. His improved method was published and patented by his US collaborator, without mentioning Heatley. However, material was not provided to the UK, and instead the UK had to manufacture its own, first for clinical trials, and, when approved, for troop use. US companies made enough for their own trials and media stunts for the miracle medicine. Florey said “after telling the Yanks every single thing we knew on the understanding that they would give us some penicillin to do some more cases . . . they have kept the lot for themselves!” By 1943 British manufactured penicillin was sufficient for the Italian campaign. The bombing of Pearl Harbor brought the USA into the war, and Uncle Sam opened his wallet to encourage the companies to engage in an unusually co-operative research and development program, with product of course reserved for US combatants. US manufactured product was eventually provided for the Normandy landings in 1944 and proved crucial in the war with Japan.

Question: Instead of citing Wikipedia which is "unreliable", can one just steal all of Wikipedia's citations from its works cited section?
Answer: Your use of the word “steal” shows your wish to cheat. You could do this, of course, but teachers are well aware of the possibility. You might consider using Wikipedia honestly. It is legitimate (and even encouraged) to use it to give yourself an overview and understanding, plus a direction to the literature for your own research. Let me give an example. Supposing I as a British person was to do a research project on preserving fish, and notice Birdseye Fish Fingers in the supermarket, so look up Fish Fingers on Wikipedia. This immediately gives me the information that they are called Fish Sticks in the USA, so I should also use this term in any searches I make. It also seems that Birdseye is not just a company name but that of Clarence Birdseye. I can click on his page and find his first patent is U.S. Patent No. 1,511,824. Typing “U.S. Patent No. 1,511,824” into my browser takes me to the text of the patent on Google Patents. I can read this - effectively an important historical document - quote from it and cite it, because I have read it. Back to the Fish Fingers page, and there are a number of links which I can click on, and quote and cite. To copy a list of references is not only cheating, it is foolish. You should only cite things you have read, and only for things they say. Wikipedia gives you a big start, but it is a help, not a substitute for thinking.

Question: When children in the 1960s were interviewed and asked what they thought life would be like in the future why were they so obsessed by the notion of atomic warfare? What was so important about atomic warfare in the 1960s?
Answer: In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis dominated the news, and it seemed like there was every chance of missile exchanges. It didn’t happen then, but the possibility remained. There was also the fear of an accidental starting of a nuclear attack through human or computer error. The 1964 film Fail Safe was about US nuclear bombers going to attack Moscow through an error in the supposed failsafe system. The film Dr Strangelove, the same year, was a black comedy, but based on familiar reality. Up to 1968 the UK had a Civil Defence Corps, and the Women’s Royal Voluntary Service, both of which were primarily concerned with helping people to survive after a nuclear attack. Many parents would be involved in these, receiving training in first-aid, dealing with radiation illness, and tricks such as making an oven out of a (metal) dustbin. Newspapers published helpful articles about the places most likely to be bombed and how far the effects would be. There was plentiful information about how to prepare if an attack seemed imminent if we had a few days, and what little you could do if an attack happened, and the government issued a warning. In the UK we had 4 minutes (the USA would have longer). We were right to be worried, but relieved when it seemed that Russia had joined the global community at last. Now we are worried again.

Question: Why do they use in the US the Fahrenheit scale when measuring temperature, while almost all the rest of the world uses the Celsius scale?
Answer: From an everyday practical point of view, the Fahrenheit scale has many advantages. 0 - 100 covers most of the ambient temperature found in inhabited areas in smaller divisions than the Celsius scale. It was adopted in meteorology for consistent records (and Fahrenheit’s thermometers were more reproducible than most of the competitors, along with the inch or mm of mercury for pressure. Like the foot or the pound it is something easy to grasp. These are less convenient if you are trying to combine units to make others. Hence scientists developed what are called coherent systems of units, the current one being the SI. I was brought up in what some call the Imperial System but changed to the SI with my involvement in science and engineering. Celsius is convenient adaptation of the Kelvin scale which has units coherent with the rest of the system. So the answer is that the USA uses °F instead of °C because they use feet instead of metres, pounds instead of kilograms etc. Despite the fact that Washington and Jefferson were enthusiasts for the metric system (casting off the oppression of the Imperial system, as they cast off the currency for a simpler revolutionary one) the customary measures stayed in place until 1866 when Congress adopted the metric system as legal throughout the states, and set up systems for their general adoption. The customary measures are legally defined as a ratio to SI ones. However, in the Land of the Free, it has been left to industry and commerce to use whichever or whatever combination they wish. Pretty much everyone else has appreciated the advantage of consistent units for trade. However the US market is so large that it is possible to run a business without worrying about foreign ideas. Certainly the media are reluctant to change their weather forecasts from what people find familiar in a competitive situation, so Fahrenheit remains.

Question: How exactly did Fritz Haber mass-produce chlorine gas in WW1? Was the Haber process used in making toxic gas? If so, how was it used to make those gas?
Answer: Fritz Haber didn’t mass produce chlorine gas. It was already being produced by the very advanced chemical industry of Germany. They were major suppliers of dyestuffs and other complicated chemicals to lots of countries. His clever idea was that as Germany (and other countries) were running short of munitions, they could use something else they already had. In addition, for this and other war gases, they had large numbers of people who were skilled with handling toxic chemicals. The only technical issue was distributing it on the battlefield. So a group of highly talented scientists carried out experiments and made calculations to determine what weather conditions and lay of the land would send the gas to the enemy. Churchill thought war gas was a brilliant idea, and asked for all resources to be provided to develop British ones. Top French chemists also went to work with enthusiasm and these three countries were soon flinging gases at each other, and developing gas masks and gases to beat gas masks. The USA developed their own toxic agent, the ‘dew of death’ which they planned to spray over German cities, but they had only just shipped it to Europe when peace broke out. The Haber-Bosch Process was solely used for munitions. Whilst the plants were being built, Germany used nitrates intended for fertilizer to make its explosives. As a result, crop yields plummeted, and Germans starved. However, after the war the process was turned mainly to fertilisers, as it is today. EDIT Germany was the only country to used phosgene as a reagent in its chemical industry, and had it in substantial amounts (plus the technicians who knew how to handle it). This was the next one to be used in December 1915, and was the gas which caused the greatest number of deaths. However France put Nobel-prize winning chemist Victor Grignard onto the job, and with other chemists devised an industrial synthesis, so were able to lob shells containing phosgene back at the Germans in February 1916.

Question: Can you give some examples of theories that have been proven wrong over time by science but remain valid for other purposes?
Answer: Let us take the stars in their courses. Theory 1: The fixed stars are in a crystal dome which rotates above the Earth. Worked great for navigation, but totally wrong. Still works for navigation. Doesn’t explain the planets at all. Theory 2: The Earth rotates around the Sun, as do the planets, according to the laws of gravity and motion put forward by Isaac Newton. Works really well to explain the planets, and you can use the maths and physics to put satellites in orbit, or even send people to the Moon. Can be used to tell you where to look for celestial phenomena. Used to calculate where the stars are in the imaginary crystal dome for navigation. Still not actually wrong, but… Theory 3: Relativity. Einstein’s view of masses affecting space-time. Gives more accurate results than Theory 2 if you are making very high-precision measurements, or going for longer distances. Not at all useful for a sailor navigating by the stars, but important for long-range space probes and the timing of satellites used for GPS. For objects in motion in everyday life and engineering, Newton’s laws are totally correct to better than our general uncertainty of working. However, there are specialist technologies where relativistic effects need to be accounted for.

Question: What is the etymology of the word god or God? Does it come from the Creator or from another source? Should we use it or not, and why?

An interesting point (for some) is that the early forms were neuter, but it was changed to masculine for the Judaeo-Christian god in Old English. The earlier Proto-Indo-European origin is debated. According to the Hebrew Bible, the name of god the creator is YHWH, with the vowels not given. This is Jehovah in the English Bible, J having been said like Y (as in the German for yes - ja.) [Exodus 6:2 - 3 And God spake unto Moses, and said unto him, I am the LORD: And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, by the name of God Almighty, but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them. This was god giving his own name. According to the Jews, this is not to be said. Adonai is an indirect reference to it as ‘the ineffable name’. Currently the best guess as to the etymology of YHWH is based on the verb to exist, so ‘the existing one’ implying always and not created unlike the universe and everything in it.

Question: Hi, what happens in the UK to a minister appointed by a PM? Does he still have also his/her function in the House of Commons or House of Lords simultaneously or is he replaced by someone else there? Do you have some sources also, where I could read more please? Thanks in advance?

Question: Now that we know the Romans used limestone and high temperature mixing to build their buildings, are we going to start using the same techniques?
Answer: They used volcanic rock (pozzolana) and lime (burnt limestone), which was available in the locality (think of Etna and Pompeii). With water these react together slowly to form a durable rock. The pozzolana is basically clay which has been subject to high temperature in a volcano. Portland cement is essentially a synthetic version of this in which clay and limestone are heated together and the melted lumps ground into powder: the two components are together, so it reacts quite quickly to form a durable rock. So yes, we know far more than they did and use their techniques in more sophisticated ways. To save energy (and CO2) we are now using some natural pozzolanas and ash from coal-fired power stations as a partial replacement in cements. Roman cement was great, but modern cements are faster and cheaper. The only problem is their great success, meaning that we have covered a lot of the world and produced a lot of CO2 in their production. For more see:

Question: Did the Nazis not really have access to oil, however their scientists had first developed how to make hydrogen fuel and hydrogen driven engines? If so, why did the Nazis need to secure the oil production of southern Russia in Op. Barbarossa?

A student who spoke Chinese and English learned Spanish from scratch and after graduation got a job with a Spanish company wanting to develop links with China. Question: Who came up with the idea of GCSE Exams? Why does the UK Government expect so much from Secondary School students? I am against this and it needs to come to an end in my opinion.
Answer: Who came up with the idea of GCSE Exams? Prior to this there were GCE O levels (General Certificate of Education) and CSEs (Certificate of Secondary Education). GCSE was essentially combing these. CSEs were a certain level of achievement, taken by less academic pupils. GCE O levels were a higher level which only the top 50% were expected to achieve. Pupils were divided into these two groups and taught accordingly. This was viewed as stigmatizing the CSE pupils. There were also arguments that some CSE pupils who did well could have done GCE O levels, while pupils who failed GCE O levels left school with nothing, when they might have achieved CSEs. Question: Why don’t gases/vapors burn above their upper flammability limit? I am not completely comfortable with the reason "gas is too rich and there is not enough air to burn".

However, the energy is spread over lots of gas molecules and the next oxygen molecule is not hot enough to react. For a flame to continue it has to be able to transfer the energy to the next combination of fuel and oxygen. If the fuel molecules are not concentrated enough you have the lower flammability limit, if the oxygen molecules are not, you have the upper limit. Note that air is mostly nitrogen. Question: What’s so difficult about converting LNG to natural gas? Can't you just let it warm up and pipe it off?
Answer: Let’s take water. To heat a kilogram of water up to 100 °C from room temperature takes the input of energy from your kettle of about 340 kJ (kilojoules). To convert that water into steam takes about 2260 kJ, nearly 7 times as long. This is the enthalpy of vaporization, also known as latent heat, and is the energy you have to give to a liquid to convert it from liquid to vapour (gas) where the molecules are much more free. This gives you an idea of the difference between warming up and boiling. With different numbers, the same is true of LNG. It needs energy to boil as well as to warm up to ambient. Since it is transported at -163 °C and is transported in highly insulated containers, this would take a long time, so we have to put energy in somehow. We do this at the rate we wish to generate the gas for our purpose.

Question: Did any of Shakespeare's literary contemporaries invent English words to the same extent that he did?

My view is that he was a popular writer, in the sense of writing to please the general population. He would deliberately use current slang, and topical phrases which his audience would immediately understand. If they were all totally new, then people would have difficulty following them. There is also a feature of English called nonce words, in which a word is made up on the spot, but is of a form that people can understand, having common components or being a variation on another word. It is like now and once. Most are just that, but if they are repeatedly invented, or the listeners are sufficiently taken with them to repeat them, then they may end up in the dictionary. An example would be ‘omnishambles’ coined in 2009 for the TV programme The Thick of It. Having said that, Shakespeare was a witty and widely educated writer, so it is likely he made up more nonce words than most, but also reflected words and wit of the time.

Question: An infant died 2 weeks after birth and it was ruled SIDS. The couple had another baby and it also died 2 weeks after birth the same way. A statistician testified this is a 1 in 73mil chance and based on this the mother went to jail. Is this fair?
Answer: It wasn’t a statistician, it was a paediatrician who awed the jury by being a Sir and a Professor, giving wrongful information in several trials, leading to wrongful convictions. He was Roy Meadows, and he was struck off the Medical Register for his actions. He stated that the chance of a cot death was 1 in 8,543 (the precision of this number immediately indicates that he was not a statistician.) Therefore the chance of two cot deaths was 8,543 x 8,543 or one in 73 million. The paper from which he took data gave a range of 214 to 8543, and Meadows took the highest figure without stating the range. He later admitted that this was his judgment - i.e. that the family was low risk. However the same factors mean they are in a group where infant murders are even rarer. There are many faults with this statement, not least the fact that it assumes the events are totally random: there is no genetic or environmental factor in common. The paper specifically cautions against this. It was concerned with understanding of public health and risk factors such as smoking. The other and more grievous one is that it is presented as the chance of the mother, Sally Clarke, being innocent of two murders. However, double murders are very rare, but no comparison of the chance of being a double murderer was made. It was presumed the only explanation for a second death. The chance of two infants dying from two different medical causes was not explored.

Question: The Bible is a masterful work of literature that has captured and stirred the minds of millions upon millions. Could it really just be made up by "uneducated" authors, or is it what it appears to be?
Answer: I doubt you have read it properly, or if you have, you haven’t read much else, otherwise you wouldn’t call it a masterful work of literature. It is a collection of old scrolls which have been joined together by committees (Jewish and Christian). In the book of Genesis in particular, even in an English translation, you can see how it jumps from one writing style to another, and from a story to a boring list. That is what it appears to be. By definition, the people who wrote these were able to write, so would be very well educated for the time. However, scholars generally suppose they were relying on oral traditions: stories, poems and family histories of fathers and fathers before, which have been important in many societies. There are also collections of wise sayings, though the Book of Proverbs is not limited to proverbs as normally considered in English, though they feature. Some include instructions from the priesthood, presumed to have been at least inspired if not directly communicated by God. These were educated people, though they only knew a tiny area of the world, and had limited understanding, so a claim that a flood covered the whole world could mean at most a very limited one. They were definitely ignorant of the solar system and what stars were. One of the problems that the committees had when deciding what the formal canon should be was that there were sometimes two scrolls telling the same story but with differences. If they could not decide between them, they included both. Thus there are two very different stories of Adam and Eve, two different versions of the Ten Commandments, and the story of Abraham pretending his wife was his sister and pimping her to a foreign king is repeated with his son, Isaac, doing the same thing with the same king with the same outcome. It is easy for critics to point to contradictions in the Bible. The New Testament contains the basic story of Jesus in the short book of Mark, then some greatly elaborated ones (most probably made up, if not by the writer, by some bloke he met who says he knew someone who swears he had a relative that had actually witnessed it.) Why some books were included (especially the mad Revelations of St John the Divine) and others which were available is a matter for discussion among scholars. No-one claims that these were uneducated people. It is ancient writings - interesting for that purpose, but they need to be viewed for what they were. Some parts can be viewed as literature, if you include poetry such as the Psalms and the Song of Solomon, but the majority is not, and its structure does not lead in any coherent and sensible manner. It is what it appears to be: an anthology of ancient writings, put together by committees having abstruse arguments in selecting what to include.

Question: How do gaseous planets (such as Uranus) implement the ideal Gas Law when there is no container for the gasses?
Answer: They don’t implement the Ideal Gas Law for the most part, because the pressure is far too high. In fact, it may be high enough for hydrogen to be a metal, which is well away from Ideal Gas behaviour. If it applies it will be in the outer atmosphere. However, the Ideal Gas Law is a pretty good fit for the atmosphere we breathe every day - from a human point of view, moderate pressure and temperature. So your question might be addressed like this: how does it work in the air outdoors when there is no container? As you are probably aware, the pressure increases under the sea, because of the weight of the water above. It goes down by about one atmosphere for every 10 metres. It is exactly the same for gas in the atmosphere. However, because water does not change its density appreciably with pressure, the weight is proportional to the depth of the water. However, air (in obedience to the Ideal Gas Law) does change its density with pressure. Therefore the density of air decreases with height, so instead of the relationship of height and pressure being a linear one, for air it is an exponential one. Thus the air gets less and less dense and there is no “top” to the atmosphere as a surface like there is with the sea. The Ideal Gas Law is commonly described in terms of a piston, but it does not require a container as such, for the following important reason. Take the classic piston and consider molecules in the middle. They are unaware of the existence of the piston, only of molecules nearby with which they are interacting. The gas law is followed whether they are in a small container or a large one, or even something as large as the atmosphere. In the atmosphere or the sea pressure is produced not by a piston just the effect of gravity on molecules above.

Question: How is the origin of sexual reproduction explained in the context of evolution? The ability to reproduce sexually isn't useful until at least 2 people can do it, and it's unlikely that two people would develop the trait at the same time (and place).
Answer: It didn’t start with people, it started with micro-organisms more than a billion years ago. Essentially it was a fault in mitosis: the process by which a cell divides by replicating its DNA so that two cells with identical genes are reproduced. The fault meant that the splitting only produced cells with half the DNA, but if two of these met, they could provide a viable organism, often with a different selection of genes. This produced mixing of genes which enabled a greater rate of evolution. Initially there were no males and females, just half-DNA cells called gametes floating about. However, through random changes some became larger, some smaller, and this is how sex is essentially defined. The female is the larger gamete, the male the smaller one. In the most primitive cases, the difference is small, but has an effect. The female can contain more material to get the new joined cell going, the male can spread more easily. Add hundreds of millions of years and we have lots of specializations such as in flowers and mammals where the male and female gametes are very different, and processes to get them together are extremely complex and varied,

Question: What category of chemicals can we synthesize already, but the cost to do so is very great?
Answer: There is no simple category. We can make many chemicals, but do not do so commercially. The obvious example is water H2O which can be made by reacting H2 with O2, but costs a lot more than using natural water. Particularly if the hydrogen is obtained from water. We can make CO2 by reacting diamonds (carbon) with oxygen but instead use that obtained from our wasteful use of fossil fuels. We can make NaCl from Na and Cl2 or NaOH and HCl, but instead get it from mines or the sea. There are many molecules which have been synthesized as a final proof of their structure so that chemists understand them. This is less common today, since we have newer methods of determining structures, but was pretty standard in the first half of the twentieth century. The first organic compound to be unequivocally synthesized was urea. Being widely available in urine, this was not for commercial reasons, but demonstrated that there was nothing special about “organic” chemicals. At that time, it was generally believed that such compounds had some life force and could only be made by a living organism. Today it is actually produced commercially by reacting ammonia NH3 with carbon dioxide CO2 in order to use it as a fertilizer and de-icing compound, because this is cheaper than extracting it from sewage. If we want more of compound found in nature, such as insulin, we are more likely to make it by biosynthesis, which typically means tweaking a micro-organism to produce it. (Actually extracting it is a big and complex chemical engineering process.) However, it and a number of other complex natural molecules were synthesized without living organisms by Bruce Merrifield in the 1960s and 70s, though these methods are not used commercially. (Developed methods might be in future.)

Question: Which British Prime Minister has been the most consequential in history?
Answer: I think Winston Churchill, but not just for what he did as PM. One of the most consequential decisions in history was made in 1912, when he was First Lord of the Admiralty, and decided (and achieved despite considerable opposition) that in future British warships would be fuelled by oil. At that time, of course, they used coal. This also meant that the Royal Navy and the British Empire to a large extent were organised around supplies of coal and places where they could be loaded onto ships, a huge logistical and strategic issue. The UK of course had its own coal, but no oil. Had the Royal Navy stuck to coal, it might not have had the success it did have in the subsequent war. Oil gave twice the energy of coal and much less smoke. It also required fewer stokers, and was quicker to load - even allowing refuelling at sea. Ships could be faster and/or better armed. The Royal Navy remained the greatest one in the world, and British power depended on it for decades. In order to secure supplies closer than the USA, in 1913 the British government took a 51% stake in Anglo-Persian Oil (which in 1954 became BP, now one of the largest energy companies in the world), and after the war was the controlling power in Iran until its independence in 1932. In the First World War the Ottoman Empire was on the side of Germany. With the end of the war, its possessions were divided up amongst the Allies. The new countries of Iraq and Palestine were created to suit Britain and France in particular. Oil supplies were a significant consideration. Oil has very much dominated world history since then. The geography of the Middle East, the relative wealth and power of different countries, and of course a number of long-running conflicts have been very much determined. Things would have been very different if Churchill had not made that one decision and been able to implement it.

Question: Did the alphabetical order of the letters in the Hebrew alphabet change over time?
Answer: No, and there is a good and very simple reason. It was also their method of counting. The first letter was used a symbol for 1, the second for 2 and so on to 10. The next letter meant 20, then 30 and so on to 100, followed by 200, 300, 400. This is 22 letters of the original alphabet. Other numbers could be got by combining in any order. A = 1, Y = 10, so AY or YA = 11 For most people in former times there would rarely be any reason to need larger numbers. Thus learning the alphabet and numbers was the same thing.

Question: Why is maths considered to be 'easier' than physics, chemistry considered to be 'easier' than physics and biology considered 'easier' than chemistry?

Not memorising, but capable of being learned by practice. This goes on as far as calculus: you can learn how to integrate or differentiate expressions without understanding what it means or why it works. Therefore some people consider it easier than physics. Many people find maths hard because they want to understand and don’t wish to just memorise. Question: Why is only one in five Muslims in the UK in full-time employment between the ages of 18 to 74? The rest are on state benefits. How much does this non-productive population cost to the UK taxpayers?

My children were not in full-time employment at the age of 18 (and a few years after) because they were students. A population with poorer health (which is often the case for financially poor groups) could mean fewer in full-time employment. 50% of the Muslim population were considered to be in poverty, compared with just under 20% of the general population. Women and older people are more likely to be in part-time employment, both associated with a degree of discrimination and family responsibilities. There are cultural reasons why this could affect the Muslim population, notably those groups with grandparents from another country who have less capability with the language. The survey found 18% of Muslim women were “looking after home and family” compared with 6% of the overall female population. Note that this alone accounts for 6 of the 15% difference between 20 and 35%. This is serious research, which deserves to be considered carefully, and not just off the cuff prejudices by armchair experts who only read the headline.

Question: History shows there were many high-ranking British military officers and politicians who came from Ireland. What drove these people to be loyal to Britain when many Irish disliked British rule?
Answer: High ranking military officers and politicians came from the wealthy land-owning class. They were generally Protestants, while the workers on their farms were Catholics, and regarded themselves as Irish. Poor people often resent rich people. There is a historical period called the Protestant Ascendency from the 17th to the early 20th century referring to this domination by people who would have identified with the ruling classes in Great Britain, not with the majority population. The Duke of Wellington, who was a great soldier but not a great Prime Minister, was born in Dublin, but went to Eton school in England, where he learned the ways of the British ruling class. You could equally look at India during the days of the British Empire, with wealthy white people born in India regarding themselves as British, while their workers may well have been resentful.

Name: Martin J Pitt
Question: Why don't British people address their elders by saying "sir" or "ma'am"?
Answer: We used to. It started going out of fashion in the 1960s. A bit more “Hey, man”, a bit less “Excuse me, sir” except for shop assistants and public servants such as police. This was something I was brought up to do (though not to address parents as anything other than Mum and Dad). Young women would be addressed as Miss. Now I would just say “Excuse me,” partly because there are now very few elders for me, and also because you can now cause offence by assuming the gender or marital status of the person you address. So most people don’t say anything.

Question: How did the United States take over the world power from Great Britain?
Answer: During the Second World War the Great Powers of Britain, Germany, France and the Soviet Union destroyed each other’s infrastructure as well as spending all their money and losing a lot of lives. Meanwhile, mainland USA was free from bombing, but the pressure of war accelerated industrial development. They sold food and goods, initially to both sides, but later only to the Allies, some of it on credit which the UK only finally paid off in 2006. The UK was shattered, while the USA had the capacity to become the ‘workshop of the world’ as the UK had been a hundred years earlier. US agriculture had also been unharmed and developed, by contrast to the destroyed fields, littered with unexploded munitions, of Europe. Following the USA entry into the war in 1941, and particularly the Pacific Theatre, it was able to use its tremendous industrial capacity (unhindered by Axis bombing) to greatly expand its Navy. By 1943 it was larger than the combined fleets of the other combatants. At the start of the war, the Royal Navy was the largest in the world. This had long been a key element in the dominance of the British Empire, not just by conquest, but by protecting trade routes. By the end of the war, the US navy was far and away the largest in the world. There was no contest. Like the UK in earlier times, the USA was now the greatest world power, militarily, industrially, and politically, and it did not hesitate to use this power to enrich itself.

Question: Can I go to more than one college in the UK at the same time?

Question: Can I get into a university without GCSE but with A levels? I have a grade 11 transcript from Africa and I am planning to take 3 A level exams.

If you are now studying in the UK, ask your school or college for help. I suggest you take a look at the website of the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (UCAS) which gives details of entry requirements for all degree courses as well as current fees and lots of other useful information and advice.

Question: If universal healthcare is so cost effective, why has the NHS costs continued to rise while the population growth has continued to decline?
Answer: You don’t understand graphs. Population growth has declined (the slope of the graph is less steep), but population has continued to rise (the graph is still going up.) Some of this is due to immigration. So the growth rate has fallen from 0.52% to 0.34%, but the population has grown from 66.8 million to 67.5 million. If the population was constant, you would still expect NHS costs to rise because of the improved technology, and new treatments, meaning that more is demanded of it. In addition, because people are living longer they receive more treatments for things like arthritis and diseases of old age.

Question: Would you rather hire a high school valedictorian with no college degree, or a college graduate with a degree unrelated to the job?

Question: As a Brit, I am turning the table on myself here. Why do we use the terms “bonnet” and ”boot” instead of “hood” and “trunk,” which clearly make more sense?
Answer: Both hood and bonnet have long been used for a protective covering over something. Control valves in chemical plants and refineries have bonnets, even in the USA. It must be a matter of chance which predominated in the two different automobile industries. Attractive though the idea of a boot trunk to store boots is, it is not supported. Early cars had a place for luggage, sometimes called a trunk rack. When a permanent compartment appeared, it was variously referred to as the deck compartment, rear trunk compartment, turtle-back or boot. According to the OED the boot was part of a coach long before cars, being from the French boîte meaning box. “The receptacle for luggage or parcels under the seats of the guard and coachman. Now the ordinary name in the U.K. for the luggage compartment usually at the rear of a motor vehicle.” Again, it is the names which happened to become the most common in the two industries, rather than any deliberate choice. The Royal Automobile Club (UK, 1897) and the American Automobile Association (USA, 1902) may have had some influence, and it would be interesting to peruse their early publications for evidence.

Question: Why does the UK not celebrate its Irish community like it does other immigrant communities?
Answer: The celebrations tend to be organized by the communities themselves. This is the longstanding Leeds Carnival (originally the Leeds West Indian Carnival) organised by people of West Indian origin in Leeds (but now featuring people from all parts of society. The LGBT+ community also organise a Pride day in Leeds and other cities. (Leeds Pride 2016. Picture by Bryan Ledgard, CC BY 2.0 <Creative Commons - Attribution 2.0 Generic - CC BY 2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons) In Bradford, which has a substantial population of South Asian Origins, there is an annual Mela, again started by people of that culture, but open to all. A number of cities have some celebration of Diwali. Leicester has a particularly large one. These days, people for whom it is important set off fireworks. In Northern Ireland there are various celebrations of the troubled history of that island in the form of parades, which lead to friction between those who identify with different factions. In the rest of the UK there are sensitivities about the killings done by the IRA and resentment about the support provided by plastic paddies in the USA. Shouting about being Irish is likely to be identified with claiming to be IRA. In addition, people whose great great grandmother lived in Ireland are unlikely to feel strongly about it, so the number of people who would identify as Irish is quite small. Celebrations tend to be confined to places such as this. The latest census shows people living in England and Wales who were born in Ireland number 325,000 out of an overall population of 60 million. By comparison 539,000 were born in Romania.

Question: Is it possible to apply to a clinical psychology PhD at the University of Oxford if I am a US citizen? If so, do the credentials transfer over to allow clinical practice in the US? Their program is only 3 years as opposed to 5-7 in the US.
Answer: It is certainly possible to apply to Oxford or any other UK university, and if you are suitable and funding is available (especially if you provide it) then you may be accepted. UK departments depend on a good fraction of their PhD students being from other countries (often the majority) in order to keep their research programmes going. Clearly entry to Oxford is going to be more competitive than some others. A PhD in the UK is shorter, because it is assumed you have had sufficient training in research to be able to start your project immediately. You commonly apply for a particular research project rather than for a general area. For international students a master’s will usually provide it. Without this, there will be some research training, and you will have to produce a document like a master’s dissertation but with your future research plan to be rigorously discussed and dissected by independent academics, after the first year in order to be permitted to proceed. There is no reason to suppose that a UK PhD will provide anything relevant to clinical practice, unless it is clearly in the research project. It is just research. However, it provides evidence of some depth and experience in the theoretical background. You should be able to look up the UK and US requirements to qualify for clinical practice on the websites of the relevant organisations, and perhaps ask the US one, which will be more authoritative than the guesses of strangers on the internet, before you commit yourself.

Question: What grades at GCSE and A level and extracurriculars do you need to get into the University of London for an undergraduate accounting and finance program?

The first page includes King’s College, Birkbeck, City, and the London School of Economics, which are all part of the University of London. It also includes other universities and institutions in the area. You can look at the rest of the pages.

Name: Martin J Pitt
Question: The Royal family in the UK still exists. They have a massive following but I don't understand it. Why is the Royal family still important to many in the UK?
Answer: Queen Elizabeths. Both of them. The late Queen Mother was also Queen Elizabeth. She was Queen of the United Kingdom and the Dominions of the British Commonwealth, and also Empress of India until it became independent. Everybody knew she wasn’t the ruler, just the consort, but there was no need to keep calling her Queen Consort like the media does with Camilla. She had been the Princess Diana of her day, a well-known society beauty, who married a pleasant but shy prince, and subsequently lived a quiet life as the Duchess of York in Mayfair, London. They had two daughters, Elizabeth and Margaret. In 1936 the shy prince unexpectedly became King George VI. This was not only unexpected, but unwelcome as they had never prepared for it, and King George had a stammer. The Duchess of York became Queen Elizabeth and supported her husband magnificently, as was widely recognised. Their two daughters got extra attention from the media, and the two princesses charmed the nation. During the Second World War the whole family stayed in London, risking the same bombs as their people, despite the government urging her and the children (at least) to go to Canada. When Buckingham Palace was bombed, she said “I'm glad we've been bombed. It makes me feel I can look the East End in the face.” Her visits to armed forces, factories and sites of destruction were much appreciated. The two princesses were also a mainstay for the media looking for good things to offset the war. Elizabeth was the charming one and Margaret the slightly naughty one, a perfect combination. The 14-year-old Elizabeth made her first radio broadcast on BBC Children’s Hour. When she was old enough, she joined the Auxiliary Territorial service, training to become an ambulance driver and mechanic. After the War, Princess Elizabeth took on various royal duties. This pretty young woman who had shared in the Blitz was probably even more welcome than her parents for the crowds. Her marriage in 1947 was a bright spot in post-war austerity. The birth of baby Charles in 1948 was another. The birth of a daughter, Anne, in 1950 could not have been better scripted for the media. The early death of her father in 1952 effectively brought an end to what limited freedom she had for a normal life, but she responded as magnificently as her mother had done to a different challenge. Up till that time, people referring to Queen Elizabeth meant her mother, who was therefore given the title of Queen Mother to reduce confusion. The Queen Mother of course provided support to her daughter in this task, but wisely kept largely quiet, just being present for those who had known her during the war, the mother of the nation. They were of my parents’ generation, who passed on their appreciation of the Royal Family to their children. In seventy years, Queen Elizabeth the Second largely acted a master class in sovereignty, combining both a respect for history and tradition with a visible humanity. A doting mother, but someone who also liked driving herself around in a Land Rover, and who could fix it as well. These two women have been the stars on which the nation’s love of the royal family has been based. The supporting actors have not always done so well, so we will see what the future brings. EDIT: On YouTube Olivia Colman reads a letter from Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother describes the experience of being bombed in 1940.

Question: Does UCL accept specifically GCSE English language resits since the website says no resits allowed but that seemed to be directed toward A levels and ICL allows them?
Answer: The point of GCSE English or an equivalent qualification is to show you have achieved a sufficient level of skill in order to be able to cope with spoken and written work at university level. It does not matter how long it took you. Once you have the certificate, that’s all the admissions office needs to tick a box. So I am sure it does not matter if it is a resit. However, your A level results are a test of your academic ability in a particular area. Some institutions will accept resits, but because entry to UCL is highly competitive, they judge you on your first attempt.

Name: Martin J Pitt
Question: Do the British view Poles as sort-of Russians?
Answer: No. The British are generally familiar with Poles. There has been a sizeable community in the UK since WW2 and many have come over in recent years and been respected as good craftsmen such as plumbers. There are many second and third generation people with Polish names and often some knowledge of the language to speak with relatives. After English, Polish is the next most common language spoken in Britain, with nearly twice as many speakers as Welsh. Polish food is available in big supermarkets, and there are Polish associations in big cities. They are generally well-liked. British people are generally unfamiliar with Russians, but our impression of them is not good, mainly due to the antics of their government, so we are unlikely to confuse the two.

Question: How can I study pure mathematics in a university with only a maths GCSE?

You will also need a third one - Physics would be good. Question: It turns out I have passed the deadlines for the applications of universities of the USA and the UK for medicine. What should I do now?
